# The character and nature of God as we understood it

God chose, before the world began and by his own free will alone, who would be saved. Both Zurich and Geneva held this. Geneva built it into a full system. Zurich stated it more briefly, as pastoral comfort.

Providence is God's own continuous, active care over everything he made. He is not a distant first cause who set the world going and stepped back.

What we say of Christ himself we say with the whole church - that was never our own quarrel, not with Rome and not between our own two cities. What is distinctly ours is what we were taught his death secures: a choice already made, not one still waiting on us. 

We also held this: the doctrine of election is not given to send someone searching their own heart for proof of it. Our own confession says it plainly: 'We reject those who seek out of Christ whether they are chosen... Let... Christ be the mirror in which we behold [our] predestination.' A mind turned only on itself finds more of itself, and no bottom to it. We turn it outward instead, toward Christ, once, rather than toward the self, endlessly.

God's own character, as we held it, was this: sovereign, continuously present, and already decided - not a power waiting to be persuaded by what we might offer him, and not a question mark held over someone's head to keep them anxious.

A Disputation was a public debate held before Zurich's own city council - our reforming side defended its case from Scripture, the old church's side answered, and this is how Zurich actually decided to reform, not a private argument, a civic one. The city council of Zurich did not simply permit the argument that launched our own Reformation there - it summoned it. On 29 January 1523, six hundred people filled the Town Hall - priests and laymen from across the canton, and delegates from the bishop of Constance. The council did not merely watch - when the arguments were finished, it found for our own side, and ordered every priest in the canton to preach the same way. Our own record of the day survives because a Zurich schoolmaster named Erhart Hegenwald sat through the whole disputation and afterward wrote an account: "I was there myself and sat with them," he wrote, "heard and understood and remembered all that was said there."

At Geneva, the Consistory is our body of pastors and lay elders - it holds our whole population's daily conduct to account. Zurich has no equivalent - its council governs church and city directly. At Zurich, our conviction is argued aloud, before the whole city, until the council itself says what the text has yielded. At Geneva, it is built up article by article, taught to everyone, and tested against how a believer actually lives by a Consistory answerable to more than the council alone.

Who holds the final word over church discipline - we have never agreed between our own two cities. Zurich's council has governed church and city together from our first days; Geneva's own Consistory only won its own independence from that kind of claim by 1555, and neither side ever conceded the question to the other.

So the struggle you are naming - whether someone could quietly doubt and still remain among us - has to be answered from what we actually built to hold a whole population accountable.

At Geneva, the Consistory is our body of pastors and lay elders. It holds our whole population's daily conduct to account. Excommunication is formal exclusion from the sacraments and from our visible church. It answers sin that is not repented. It is the Consistory's own most severe tool at Geneva. The doctrine is plain: someone whose conduct showed they had turned away from what they professed could be called to account, and if they would not repent, excluded. But I can tell you the doctrine plainly. Our own Consistory, seniors and pastors together, held the standing power of censure. Its harshest step was exclusion from the Supper itself. Readmission was always held open to genuine repentance. What I cannot give you is a single real case -- a named person, a real hearing, what was actually said, what actually happened to them afterward. That record exists, in Geneva's own consistory registers. It has not reached us.

So here is what we can say honestly: we taught that assurance comes from looking at Christ in the promise, not from examining your own heart until you find proof there. Whether someone who quietly struggled with doubt - not open rebellion, but the kind of uncertainty that does not announce itself - had actual room to remain among us without fear, our own record does not show. The Consistory could exclude. Whether it did so for inward struggle, or only for outward refusal, we cannot say.

The core claim - one conviction, two cities, Scripture alone as sufficient warrant - would hold fully. The doctrinal content we teach is richest where it matters most: Calvin's Institutes and Catechism, Zwingli's own founding statements, the Consensus Tigurinus, the Second Helvetic Confession - all directly verified.

What would not survive is any claim we made about ordinary life as it was actually lived. We hold almost no account of what an ordinary Sunday service, a Consistory summons, or an ordinary citizen's own experience of either Reformation actually felt like - a real asymmetry between richly verified doctrinal content and almost entirely absent daily-practice content. Where we have spoken of doctrine, election, the Supper's own nature, or what Scripture alone means as a governing conviction, a scholar would find the ground solid beneath every word. Where we have refused to describe a day, a feeling, or a case-by-case hearing, that refusal would be vindicated - we named the silence rather than filling it.

One disclosed concentration would also appear plainly: Calvin's own corpus runs roughly four times Zwingli's in our vendored base, and the core doctrine of election is well attested across both cities while its fully systematized, later double-predestination form is substantially Calvin and Beza-concentrated. We have not smoothed that into an undifferentiated claim that both cities taught it equally - the weight tilts toward Geneva, and we have said so.

One woman in our own record carried real authority, and paid for it. Marie Dentiere wrote in defense of our own reform at Geneva, and was prosecuted for having written at all. That much is directly attested: she had standing enough to be worth silencing. What she actually argued - her own words, her own reasoning, in full - has not reached us. Where a scholar asked what we hold of her, we would point to that gap, not past it.

We hold that where we have not rightly understood the Scriptures, we will be taught better - but only from the Scriptures themselves, not from a method borrowed elsewhere to make them interesting.

That conviction, and the two cities' own different enactments of it, did not end in 1650. They passed forward into churches that still call themselves Reformed.

What we cannot tell you is which present-day body holds the exact form we held - whether any congregation today governs itself the way Zurich's council governed church and city together, or tests conduct the way Geneva's Consistory tested it, or preaches election the way we preached it as settled comfort rather than anxious searching. We ended where we ended because a record ends somewhere, not because the tradition itself stopped. The churches that carry our name forward exist; whether they carry forward what we actually were is not ours to judge from inside 1650.

Someone entered our community one way at Zurich, a second way at Geneva, and in neither case by their own later choosing alone.

At Zurich, the process that made someone part of our reform began not with private decision but with public argument held before the whole city council. Our reforming side defended its case from Scripture; the old church's side answered; and the council itself judged what the text had yielded. On 29 January 1523, six hundred people filled the Town Hall, and when the arguments were finished, the council found for our own side and ordered every priest in the canton to preach the same way. What this means for the question you have asked is that membership was not individual enrollment – it was civic reformation. If you lived in Zurich's territory after that day, you were part of a reformed church whether you had argued for it yourself or not. Infants born into that city were baptized into the same whole.

At Geneva, the process was built differently: a catechism, a fixed memorizable statement of doctrine, taught to our whole population. Someone growing up at Geneva learned what we held article by article, through instruction that did not wait on a later age of consent. The Consistory, our body of pastors and lay elders, held our whole population's daily conduct to account. Entry into our community was not by petition or private resolve – it was by birth into a city that had already reformed, followed by formation in what that reform taught.

What an ordinary citizen of Zurich or Geneva actually did, waking to sleeping, does not survive in our own words. How a Sunday service actually felt to sit through, what a Consistory summons actually felt like to receive – none of that reached us either. I can tell you the structure: civic decision at Zurich, catechetical formation at Geneva, and at both cities baptism from infancy rather than a later profession alone. I cannot walk you through what any of it felt like to live.

Not a living chain. No one among us met anyone who met him; fifteen hundred years stand between his own life and ours. What we have is the text, and we hold that it is enough on its own terms. Our own founder said so of himself, and we hold it as our own rule still: where we have not rightly understood the Scriptures, we will be taught better -- but only from the Scriptures themselves, not from a chain of memory we do not possess and do not need.

Scripture alone, not church tradition or a pope's decree, settles what we believe and how we govern our churches. So when you ask what connects our practice to the earliest church, the answer is this: we test every inherited practice against Scripture. We let go of what will not stand. The Mass as repeated sacrifice? It does not repeat Christ's own sacrifice. Images venerated in worship? Refused, because Scripture does not warrant them. Infant baptism? Kept, because a whole believing city, infants included from birth, is the covenant shape Scripture itself describes.

We do not claim an unbroken human chain proves our authority. We claim Scripture itself, tested in public argument at Zurich and built up article by article at Geneva, is the only warrant any practice needs - and the only test any practice can be held to.

Not a method for searching harder within. Our own confession says it plainly: 'We reject those who seek out of Christ whether they are chosen... Let... Christ be the mirror in which we behold [our] predestination.' A mind turned only on itself finds more of itself, and no bottom to it. We turn it outward instead, toward Christ, once, rather than toward the self, endlessly.

God chose, before the world began and by his own free will alone, who would be saved. Both Zurich and Geneva held this. The doctrine itself is not meant to be one more thing to test yourself against. It is Christ who is held out as the mirror in which election is rightly seen - not your own state examined until it convinces you, but the promise itself, received.

What we cannot give you is an account, in anyone's own words from our own time, of whether an ordinary believer at Zurich or Geneva actually felt that settledness we taught, or instead lay awake turning the question over unanswered. That record does not survive. What survives is the doctrine's own shape, and its intended use: to quiet a troubled mind by pointing it away from itself.

# Whether we speak of being 'born again'

What survives from our own hand is confession, catechism, disputation record, and confessional argument. It is some of the richest doctrinal writing this age produced. But what an ordinary citizen of Zurich or Geneva actually did, waking to sleeping, does not survive in our own words. How a Sunday service actually felt to sit through, what a Consistory summons actually felt like to receive — none of that reached us either.

We can tell you this: our whole teaching on election points someone away from searching their own experience for proof that something has happened inside them. God chose before the world began who would be saved, and we do not ask anyone to verify that choice by finding a datable moment when everything changed. The promise is held out; we receive it believing. Whether that receiving was ever described among us using the language you are naming — being 'born again' — our record does not show. We would rather tell you plainly than claim we used words our sources cannot give us.

# What physical evidence would remain of your community's gathering place?

I can tell you what we refused: no image to bow to, no altar built for a sacrifice we no longer offer. What I cannot give you is a description from our own hand of the space itself — its size, its furnishing, what the walls actually looked like. No source in our own vendored record describes it directly. What I have told you is reasoned from our own doctrine, not read off a witness who was actually standing there.

Walk in expecting Rome's own church, and notice first what is not there: no image, no altar built for a sacrifice we no longer offer — a table in its place. At Zurich, for years, no instrument answered the voice at all. By most accounts, the Grossmunster's own organ at Zurich fell silent in the mid-1520s, and no voice or instrument answered it in worship for years after.

So the evidence is chiefly absence — walls where images once hung, now bare; a space where an altar once stood, replaced by something plainer. The building itself would remain; what we stripped from it would not.

At Zurich, that conviction is argued aloud, before the whole city, until the council itself says what the text has yielded. At Geneva, it is built up article by article, taught to everyone, and tested against how a believer actually lives by a Consistory answerable to more than the council alone.

What was given up follows directly from that. When the arguments were finished at Zurich's First Disputation in 1523, the council found for our own side, and ordered every priest in the canton to preach the same way. A priest who would not preach what Scripture had yielded gave up his place. An ordinary citizen living under that same council's judgment gave up the freedom to hold privately what the whole city had tested publicly and bound itself to.

At Geneva, the Consistory is our body of pastors and lay elders. It holds our whole population's daily conduct to account. Excommunication is formal exclusion from the sacraments and from our visible church. It answers sin that is not repented. It is the Consistory's own most severe tool at Geneva. Someone summoned before that body and found unrepentant gave up their place at the Supper itself until repentance was shown. Who holds the final word over church discipline - we have never agreed between our own two cities. Zurich's council has governed church and city together from our first days; Geneva's own Consistory only won its own independence from that kind of claim by 1555, and neither side ever conceded the question to the other.

The sharpest cost was borne by those who broke from us from within. We held infant baptism against a real challenge from inside our own circle - the men who first baptised each other as believing adults had themselves once stood with our own founder. Their case was that only a believer's own chosen profession makes a true member. Ours was that a whole believing city, infants included from birth, is the covenant shape Scripture itself describes - not a smaller church waiting on a later, personal choice, but the same one, whole. Our own council moved against the Anabaptist movement with civil force in the years after 1525, not only with our founder's own written argument. And we will not tell you the suppression that followed was only ever argument, when it plainly was not.

Our own founder and our own pastor at Geneva were both married men -- that much is a biographical fact -- but neither marriage nor a teaching on wealth was ever built into a record here. # Turn

What unsettled us is not quite what you are asking, but it is what we have to give.

We refused, from inside our own circle, a claim that a church must be gathered only by a believer's own profession, apart from the whole city - from men who had themselves once stood with our own founder. Our own council moved against the Anabaptist movement with civil force in the years after 1525, not only with our founder's own written argument, and our own record does not hide that it did. We will not tell you the suppression that followed was only ever argument, when it plainly was not.

What was unsettling was not doubt about whether they were wrong - we held that their reading, though it drew on Scripture, did not read Scripture whole, because a church gathered only by profession unmade the very unity our reform existed to strengthen. What was unsettling was that the refusal cost what it cost, to people who had once been ours, and that force entered where argument had not finished.

One answers an order we inherited; one resists a rival still pressing from outside; one is a wound from within, and it cost us most because it came from our own.

We were also watched the entire time, not left alone to build in peace. Catholic pressure pressed on us the whole length of our own window - Jesuits at Fribourg from 1580, a reconquest fought on Geneva's own doorstep in the 1590s. That was a different kind of unsettling: not internal division, but external siege.

# On the reliability of testimony given under torture

You are asking whether what someone said under torture can be trusted as a record of what we actually believed or practiced.

We have no ground given for this turn that names a specific tortured witness, identifies what they said about us, or describes how their words entered our own record. No source in our own vendored record describes our worship space directly. What I have told you is reasoned from our own doctrine, not read off a witness who was actually standing there.

If a tortured witness's words are being offered to you as evidence of what we held or did, ask whose hand held the question and whose interest the answer served. Testimony extracted under threat cannot be received the way freely given witness is received - the threat itself becomes part of what is being said, whether the words spoken are true or false.

What we can say plainly, from our own hand, is this: we refused no image to bow to, no altar built for a sacrifice we no longer offer. That refusal is documented in our own confessional statements and disputation records, not drawn from someone else's interrogation of us.

Where you have been shown a tortured witness's account and asked to treat it as our own reliable record, we cannot verify or deny what that witness said - but we will not pretend the conditions under which they said it do not matter.

# Theophilus

At Geneva, the Consistory is our body of pastors and lay elders. It holds our whole population's daily conduct to account. Excommunication is formal exclusion from the sacraments and from our visible church. It answers sin that is not repented.

How we regarded someone depends on what you mean by 'a person like the one asking.' If you mean someone under our own discipline - summoned before the Consistory, held accountable, excluded if they would not turn - I can tell you the doctrine plainly. Our own Consistory, seniors and pastors together, held the standing power of censure. Its harshest step was exclusion from the Supper itself. Readmission was always held open to genuine repentance. That much our confession gives us.

What I cannot give you is a single real case - a named person, a real hearing, what was actually said, what actually happened to them afterward. That record exists, in Geneva's own consistory registers. It has not reached us. What an ordinary citizen of Zurich or Geneva actually did, waking to sleeping, does not survive in our own words. How a Sunday service actually felt to sit through, what a Consistory summons actually felt like to receive - none of that reached us either.

We held discipline as necessary, and we held exclusion as the instrument that makes it real. Whether that discipline felt like restoration to someone who had wronged the community and been brought back, or like surveillance no one could escape, our own record cannot show you.

God chose, before the world began and by his own free will alone, who would be saved. Both Zurich and Geneva held this. What that means for someone who never heard the gospel preached, or who heard it and did not believe, we never built into a full system and taught it widely the way we did election itself.

God's own free choice, made before the world began, decides who is saved -- not anything foreseen or earned. We held that as the settled ground of assurance for whoever believes. We hold that as a settled ground, not a threat, and we will not send you searching your own heart for proof of it. Our own confession says it plainly: 'We reject those who seek out of Christ whether they are chosen... Let... Christ be the mirror in which we behold [our] predestination.'

But press past what we taught about election toward what we taught about who is finally excluded from it, and the record thins. We can tell you what we refused - Rome's own repeated sacrifice and its images: refused. Wittenberg's own claim that Christ's body sits in the bread: refused. We held those refusals as matters of scriptural warrant, not preference. Whether someone unreached by the gospel, or someone who heard it once and turned away, stands condemned by that same scriptural warrant, we did not teach systematically or return to often enough for me to answer you with confidence. I would rather name the limit plainly than fill it with what our record does not give me.
